title: The Three Themes and All Topics
summary: The three themes and every topic behind all four 9280 papers, with a word bank and ready-to-use ideas for each topic.

blocks.text: Every part of the 9280 exam is built on **three themes**. The reading texts, the writing tasks, the listening recordings and the speaking photocards all come from these themes. This page gives you every topic, a word bank for each one, and ready-made ideas you can use in any paper. Learn the words in sentences, not alone.
The three themes at a glance

rows: Me, my family, friends and people I know
Relationships with family, and relationships with friends and people I know
Music, cinema and TV, sport, and customs and festivals
2 Local, national, international and global areas of interest
Where you live and what it is like
3 Current and future study and employment
The school day, rules, activities, pressures
What you study after 16: sixth form, college, university, apprenticeships

blocks.text: How the themes appear in each paper

rows: All four texts are linked to the themes, e.g. an email about a charity event, an advert for holiday activities, an article about careers, a travel memoir.
Knowing theme vocabulary makes texts faster to read and helps you guess unknown words.
Questions 1, 2 and 3 are each based on one theme. Question 4 can draw on one or more themes.
Have ideas ready for each topic so you never sit with an empty page.
All five tasks are linked to the themes: everyday announcements, interviews, talks, podcasts.
Theme words help you catch key details on the first listening.
The photocard covers one theme. The conversation covers the other two themes.
You must be ready to talk about ALL three themes, because you do not choose.

blocks.title: How to study this page
items: Take one topic a day. Read the word bank aloud. Cover the meanings and test yourself.
Write five sentences about YOUR life using new words from the topic.
Use the 'ideas' lists as building blocks: each idea can become a paragraph in writing or a one-minute answer in speaking.
Look for the same words when you read English articles. Real texts repeat theme vocabulary all the time.

blocks.text: THEME 1: Identity and culture

This theme is about you: the people in your life, how you use technology, and what you do for fun. It is the most personal theme, so it is easy to use in Speaking and in personal writing such as blogs, diaries and letters.
Topic 1.1 Me, my family, friends and people I know
Sub-topics: relationships with family, and relationships with friends and people I know. Expect texts and questions about who you are close to, arguments, support, role models and growing up.

items: argue and stop being friends for a time
become friends again after an argument
a family whose members support each other
a child with no brothers or sisters
a person you admire and want to copy
differences in ideas between young and old people
you can depend on them; they keep secrets
pressure from people your age to behave like them
someone you know, but not well
care for a child until adulthood
being free to make your own decisions

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: Family gives security and advice, but teenagers also need independence and privacy.
A good friend is loyal, honest and supportive in difficult times, not only in good times.
Grandparents pass on traditions and experience; the generation gap can be closed by spending time together.
A role model does not have to be famous: a parent, teacher or older sibling can inspire us most.

blocks.text: Topic 1.2 Technology in everyday life
Sub-topics: social media and mobile technology. This topic often appears as an opinion article with good and bad points, which is perfect for collation (list) questions.

items: a website or app for sharing, e.g. a photo app
put a photo or message online
spread very quickly to millions of people online
keeping your personal information safe online
the time spent looking at a phone or computer
a message that pops up on your phone
take from / put on the internet
a secret word to protect an account
a person who affects what followers buy or think
stop using a device, or relax

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: Mobile phones keep families in touch and help students learn, for example with dictionary apps and online lessons.
Too much screen time can damage sleep, concentration and physical health.
Social media lets young people share ideas and support charities, but it can also spread fake news and cyberbullying.
The answer is balance: phone-free times such as meals and an hour before bed.

blocks.text: Topic 1.3 Free-time activities
Sub-topics: music, cinema and TV, sport, and customs and festivals. Adverts and brochures for activities (Text 2 style) and diary/blog writing about a celebration can appear here.

items: an activity you do for pleasure
a service that plays films or music online
a TV programme in parts / one part
music performed in front of an audience
a type of music or film, e.g. comedy, rock
the feeling of working together in a team
a person who watches a sport
something people have done for a long time
a special day or event of happiness
make a place look attractive for an event

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: Hobbies reduce stress after school and help us make friends with the same interests.
Team sports teach cooperation, discipline and how to accept losing.
Festivals such as Eid bring families together: visiting relatives, special food, new clothes and gifts for children.
Streaming is convenient, but watching a film at the cinema with friends is a shared experience.

blocks.text: THEME 2: Local, national, international and global areas of interest

This theme moves from your home to the whole world: your town, helping others, health, the environment, poverty and travel. Opinion articles (Text 3) and literary travel writing (Text 4) often come from here.
Topic 2.1 Home, town, neighbourhood and region
Expect descriptions of places, advantages and disadvantages of city and village life, and improvements to your area.

items: an area with mainly houses and flats
areas at the edge of a city
the main, busy part of a city
a long line of cars that cannot move
places and services, e.g. sports centres, libraries
calm and quiet / full of activity
the people who live in an area
of the countryside / of the city
a group of new homes built together with shared services

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: City life offers jobs, shops and entertainment, but brings noise, pollution and traffic.
Village or suburb life is calmer and greener, though facilities and transport may be limited.
My area could be improved with more green spaces, cycle lanes and youth clubs.
A good neighbourhood is safe, clean and friendly, with people who help each other.

blocks.text: Topic 2.2 Social issues
Sub-topics: charity/voluntary work and healthy/unhealthy living. Charity events, sponsored challenges, diets and exercise can appear in emails and articles.

items: an organisation that helps people in need
a person who works without pay / to do this
promise money if someone completes a challenge
give money or things / the gift
help the community that helped you
food with the right mix of nutrients
unhealthy food with much fat, sugar or salt
the health of your mind and feelings
a life with too much sitting
sleep the hours your body needs

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: Volunteering helps others and gives young people skills, confidence and experience for their CV.
Even small actions help: collecting clothes, visiting the elderly, a sponsored walk.
A healthy life needs a balanced diet, regular exercise, enough sleep and time away from screens.
Schools could help by selling healthy snacks and offering more sports clubs.

blocks.text: Topic 2.3 Global issues
Sub-topics: the environment and poverty. These topics suit Writing Question 4 (argue or persuade) and opinion articles in Reading.

items: gases that trap heat, e.g. carbon dioxide
the amount of carbon your activities produce
energy that does not run out, e.g. solar, wind
the three ways to cut waste
plastic used once and thrown away
animals or plants that may disappear
no rain for a long time / too much water
can continue without harming the planet
food, water, shelter and health care
a country with less money and industry
help, often money or food, for people in need
the chance to go to school

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: Individuals can help the environment: recycling, using less plastic, saving water and electricity, walking instead of driving.
Governments should invest in renewable energy and public transport.
Education is the strongest way to break the cycle of poverty.
Rich countries and charities can provide aid, but long-term jobs and fair pay matter most.

blocks.text: Topic 2.4 Travel and tourism
Holiday adverts and brochures (Text 2) and travel memoirs (Text 4) are typical. Writing Question 1 photographs may look as if they come from a holiday brochure or travel blog.

items: a place to stay, e.g. a hotel
a holiday with flight and hotel together
away from places most tourists go
something you buy to remember a place
the remains of very old buildings
a visit led by a guide
travel that protects nature and helps local people
tiredness after a long flight across time zones
the amount of money you plan to spend
learn about new ideas and cultures

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: Travel broadens your horizons: new cultures, languages, food and friends.
Tourism brings jobs and money, but too many tourists can damage historic sites and nature.
Egypt has world-famous attractions: the pyramids, Luxor's temples and the Red Sea coast.
A holiday at home (exploring your own country) can be cheaper and greener than flying abroad.

blocks.text: THEME 3: Current and future study and employment
This theme is about your studies now and your plans for the future. Letters to parents about school events, reports on school activities and articles about careers or apprenticeships are typical.
Topic 3.1 My studies
Subjects you like and dislike, how you learn best, homework, revision and exams.

items: a subject you must / can choose to study
the plan of lessons in the week
a plan for when to revise each subject
a piece of work set by a teacher
the last date to hand in work
succeed / not succeed in an exam
a teacher for one student or a small group
the way you learn best, e.g. by seeing or doing

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: My favourite subject is useful for my future career and taught in an interesting way.
A revision schedule, short breaks and past papers help students prepare for exams.
Some students learn best in groups, others alone and in silence.
Exams create stress, but good planning and sleep reduce it.

blocks.text: Topic 3.2 Life at school/college
The school day, rules, uniforms, clubs, trips, events and the pressure students feel.

items: the hours of lessons and breaks
what you must do / obeying rules
a visit to a place with your class
a day of sports races / swimming races
a meeting of the whole school
the person in charge of a school
e.g. a science lab, library, playground
a feeling that you must do well
hurting or frightening a weaker person again and again
a meeting between teachers and parents
the place to buy and eat food at school

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: Clubs and trips make school more enjoyable and build friendships and confidence.
School uniform creates equality and saves time, though some say it limits self-expression.
A school council lets students share ideas and improve their school.
Long school days and homework can leave little time for rest and hobbies.

blocks.text: Topic 3.3 Education post-16
What students do after 16: staying at school or sixth form, going to college, university, apprenticeships or training.

items: the last two years of secondary school in the British system
a course that trains you for a particular job
a job with training; you earn while you learn
a qualification after studying at university
a person with a degree / finish university
money paid for teaching at a college or university
money to pay for study, given for good results or need
the grades you need to be accepted
a year off between school and university
the buildings and land of a university
money borrowed to study / money you owe

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: University opens doors to professions such as medicine and engineering, but it is expensive.
Apprenticeships give practical skills and a salary with no student debt.
A gap year can build maturity through travel or volunteering, but some students lose motivation.
Studying abroad improves your English and independence, but you may miss your family.

blocks.text: Topic 3.4 Jobs, career choices and ambitions
Part-time jobs, work experience, dream careers and what makes a job good.

items: the work you do for most of your life
work for some / all of the week
a short time working to learn about a job
money you earn (monthly / hourly or weekly)
the person who gives work / the person who works
a strong wish to achieve something
a document listing your education and experience
a meeting to decide if you get the job
moving to a higher position at work
time for work and time for family and rest
the route of jobs you take over time

blocks.title: Ideas you can use
items: My ambition is to become an engineer because I enjoy solving problems and want to build useful things.
A good job offers a fair salary, job satisfaction and a healthy work-life balance.
Part-time jobs and work experience teach responsibility and time management.
Skills such as teamwork, communication and technology are important in every career.

blocks.text: Use one idea in all four papers
Here is how one idea from Topic 2.2 (volunteering) can help you everywhere:

rows: You meet 'raise funds', 'sponsor', 'volunteers' in an email about a charity walk and understand them instantly.
Q2 letter: invite parents to a charity concert. Q4: explain why young people should volunteer.
An interview with a teenage volunteer: you catch 'donations' and 'the elderly' easily.
Photocard of students cleaning a beach: describe it, then give your opinion with reasons.

items.q: Which theme does a text about choosing between university and an apprenticeship belong to?
items.a: Theme 3 (Current and future study and employment), topic: Education post-16.

items.q: Your speaking photocard is about Theme 2. Which themes will the general conversation cover?
items.a: Theme 1 (Identity and culture) and Theme 3 (Current and future study and employment): the two themes NOT on the photocard.

items.q: Give a word that means 'give money to a charity'.
What is the difference between 'salary' and 'wage'?
items.a: Both mean money from work. A salary is usually a fixed yearly amount paid monthly, while a wage is usually paid by the hour or week.
A place away from the usual tourist areas, not visited by many people.

items.q: Give two disadvantages of social media and one solution.
items.a: For example: (1) cyberbullying and (2) too much screen time, which harms sleep. Solution: phone-free times, such as an hour before bed.

blocks.title: كيف تذاكر المحاور الثلاثة؟
items: لا تحفظ الكلمات منفصلة؛ اكتب كل كلمة في جملة عن حياتك أنت.
ذاكر موضوعًا واحدًا كل يوم، وراجع القديم مرة في الأسبوع.
في امتحان المحادثة لا تختار الموضوع، لذلك جهّز أفكارًا للمحاور الثلاثة كلها.
الفكرة الواحدة تنفعك في الأربع ورقات: القراءة والكتابة والاستماع والمحادثة.
